history:6.sub: From petitions to Poorna Swaraj: India's long road to 15 August 1947

p: In December 1885, a small group of educated Indians gathered in Bombay and founded the Indian National Congress. A retired British civil servant, A.O. Hume, helped bring the group together, and W.C. Bonnerjee presided over the first session.

The early leaders, known as the Moderates, included Dadabhai Naoroji, G.K. Gokhale and Pherozeshah Mehta. They trusted constitutional methods such as petitions, speeches and resolutions. Naoroji's drain of wealth theory showed how British rule steadily carried India's resources out of the country.

n.x: Moderates believed in petitions and prayers. The Extremists, who came later, believed in boycott and self-reliance.

s.h: Partition of Bengal and the Swadeshi Wave
p: In 1905 the Viceroy Lord Curzon divided Bengal into two parts, officially for administrative convenience. Indians saw it as a plan to split Hindus from Muslims, and the reaction was explosive. The Swadeshi movement urged people to use Indian goods, while the Boycott of British cloth spread across the country.

This phase gave rise to the Extremists, remembered as Lal-Bal-Pal: Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Bipin Chandra Pal. Tilak's cry that Swaraj was his birthright became a rallying call. The Muslim League was formed in 1906, and in 1907 the Congress split at Surat between the Moderates and the Extremists.

s.h: Gandhi Enters: The Age of Mass Movements
p: Mahatma Gandhi returned from South Africa in 1915. His first satyagrahas in India were at Champaran (1917), Kheda and Ahmedabad (1918). Then came the Rowlatt Act of 1919, which allowed detention without trial. During the protests, General Dyer's troops fired on an unarmed crowd at Jallianwala Bagh, Amritsar, on 13 April 1919.

Gandhi answered with the Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-22), which he withdrew after violence at Chauri Chaura. In 1930 he led the Dandi March from Sabarmati to the sea to break the salt law, beginning the Civil Disobedience Movement.

The Cripps Mission of 1942 failed to satisfy Indian leaders. In August 1942 Gandhi gave the call Do or Die at Bombay, launching the Quit India Movement. Most leaders were arrested at once, yet the movement spread widely on its own.
After the Second World War, the Cabinet Mission of 1946 prepared the ground for a transfer of power. India became independent on 15 August 1947, together with the pain of Partition.

n.x: Learn this year chain: 1885, 1905, 1919, 1930, 1942, 1947. Most questions test these dates.

sum: The Congress was founded in 1885; Hume was a key founder.
The Partition of Bengal (1905) by Curzon sparked Swadeshi.
Jallianwala Bagh (1919) and Dandi March (1930) are major turning points.
Quit India (1942) gave the slogan Do or Die.
Independence came on 15 August 1947.

history:0.sub: One of the world's first great urban cultures, built on grids, bricks and trade

p: The civilization was first noticed at Harappa in 1921 and then at Mohenjo-daro in 1922, which is why it is also called the Harappan Civilization. Its mature phase lasted from about 2600 to 1900 BCE, and it belongs to the Bronze Age.
Its settlements stretched across present-day Pakistan and north-western India, along the Indus and the now-dry Ghaggar-Hakra river.

What amazes historians is the town planning. Streets met at right angles in a grid pattern, houses were built of burnt bricks, and a system of covered drains carried waste water away. Most cities were divided into a raised citadel and a lower town.
At Mohenjo-daro stands the famous Great Bath, probably used for ritual bathing. Large granaries have been found at Harappa.

n.x: Great Bath = Mohenjo-daro. Dockyard = Lothal. Fire altars = Kalibangan.

p: Hundreds of sites have been found. The table lists the ones that appear again and again in exams.

The people grew wheat, barley and cotton, and kept cattle, sheep and goats. Craftsmen worked with copper, bronze, gold and silver, but iron was unknown. Square stone seals made of steatite carried animal figures and a script that nobody has yet deciphered.
Traders exchanged goods with Mesopotamia by land and sea, and Lothal's dockyard shows how important sea trade was.

n.x: A favourite question: which metal was not known to the Harappans? The answer is iron.

sum: Harappa was found in 1921 and Mohenjo-daro in 1922.
Cities followed a grid plan with burnt bricks and covered drains.
Lothal had a dockyard; Kalibangan had fire altars.
Copper, bronze and gold were used; iron was not.

geography:2.sub: The lifelines of India: how rivers shape land, farming and cities

p: Indian rivers fall into two groups. The Himalayan rivers, the Indus, the Ganga and the Brahmaputra, are perennial: they are fed by both rain and melting snow, so they carry water all year.
The Ganga, about 2,500 km long, is the longest river flowing mostly within India. Its important tributaries include the Yamuna, Ghaghara, Gandak and Kosi.

Rivers of the peninsula depend on monsoon rain, so their flow rises and falls with the seasons. Because the Deccan plateau slopes towards the east, most of them, such as the Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri and Mahanadi, flow into the Bay of Bengal.

The Godavari is the longest peninsular river and is called Dakshin Ganga. Two rivers behave differently: the Narmada and Tapi flow west through rift valleys and fall into the Arabian Sea, forming estuaries instead of deltas.

n.x: Narmada and Tapi are the two big west-flowing rivers of the peninsula.

p: Lakes may be freshwater, saline or coastal lagoons. Wular Lake in Jammu and Kashmir is commonly cited as the largest freshwater lake, while Chilika in Odisha is a brackish water lagoon and a famous bird habitat.

sum: Himalayan rivers are perennial; peninsular rivers are rain-fed.
The Ganga is the longest river within India; the Godavari is the longest peninsular river.
Narmada and Tapi flow west into the Arabian Sea.
Chilika is a lagoon in Odisha; Wular is a freshwater lake in J&K.

biology:3.sub: The remarkable journey of a meal, from your first bite to the last nutrient

p: Food travels through the alimentary canal: mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine and anus. Along the way the body carries out five steps: ingestion, digestion, absorption, assimilation and egestion.
Digestion is both mechanical, as teeth chew and muscles churn, and chemical, as enzymes break big molecules into small ones that the blood can carry.
Digestion begins in the mouth. Saliva contains salivary amylase, an enzyme that starts turning starch into sugar. Waves of muscle movement, called peristalsis, push food down the oesophagus.

In the stomach, gastric juice does the work. Hydrochloric acid kills germs and creates the right conditions for pepsin, an enzyme that digests proteins. Mucus protects the stomach wall from its own acid.

s.h: The Small Intestine: Where Absorption Happens
p: The small intestine is the longest part of the canal and the main site of digestion and absorption. Its inner wall is covered with finger-like villi that increase the surface area for absorbing nutrients.

The liver, the largest gland of the body, makes bile, which is stored in the gall bladder. Bile does not contain enzymes, but it breaks fat into tiny droplets. The pancreas adds juice containing trypsin, lipase and amylase.
What remains passes into the large intestine, which absorbs most of the remaining water and forms solid waste that leaves the body through the anus.

n.x: Remember: most absorption is in the small intestine, water absorption is in the large intestine.

sum: Digestion starts in the mouth with salivary amylase.
The stomach secretes HCl and pepsin.
Most digestion and absorption occurs in the small intestine.
The liver is the largest gland; bile is stored in the gall bladder.

reasoning:1.sub: Crack the secret rule behind every coded word

p: In coding-decoding questions, a word or number is changed into a code using a hidden rule. You are shown one example, and you must discover the rule and use it on a new word. The rule is nearly always simple, so the skill lies in spotting it quickly.
The most common rule moves every letter a fixed number of steps along the alphabet. In CAT to DBU, each letter moves one step forward. Using the same rule, DOG becomes EPH.
Sometimes letters are replaced by their position numbers, where A=1, B=2 and so on up to Z=26. Opposite letters, such as A and Z or B and Y, always add up to 27.

n.x: Memorise EJOTY: E=5, J=10, O=15, T=20, Y=25. It helps you count positions fast.

p: Another rule writes the letters in reverse order, so PEN becomes NEP. Some questions mix two rules, for example reversing the word and then shifting every letter. When that happens, test each rule on its own first.
First compare the first letter of the word with the first letter of its code to see the shift. Then check that the same rule fits the other letters. Finally, apply it to the new word.
Worked example: if MANGO is coded as NBOHP, each letter moves one step ahead, so APPLE is coded as BQQMF.

sum: Find the rule from the given example.
Common rules are +1, -1, reversal and position numbers.
Opposite letters add up to 27.
Always test the rule on every letter.

mathematics:1.sub: The foundation of profit and loss, interest and data interpretation

p: The word percent means per hundred. So 25% means 25 out of every 100. To find x% of a number N, multiply N by x and divide by 100.
To express one number as a percentage of another, use (obtained / total) × 100. A student who scores 360 out of 600 has scored 60%.
Learning a few fractions saves a lot of time. Instead of multiplying by 25 and dividing by 100, just divide by 4.
To find how much a value has grown or fallen, use % change = (change / original) × 100. Always divide by the original value, not the new one.
If a price rises from ₹200 to ₹250, the change is 50 and the base is 200, so the increase is 25%.
Sometimes the percentage and its value are given, and you must find the full number. If x% of a number is V, then the number equals V × 100 / x.
For example, if 40% of a number is 80, the number is 80 × 100 / 40 = 200.

n.x: Always convert the percentage to a simple fraction first. It is faster and less error-prone.

sum: x% of N = x × N / 100.
Learn fraction equivalents like 25% = 1/4.
% change = change / original × 100.
If x% of a number is V, the number is V × 100 / x.
